Borderline Claims: South Africans and asylum in Europe

By: Nickolaus Bauer | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Are South Africans fleeing danger — or gaming Europe’s asylum system to escape inequality at home?

Unique Selling Point:
Carte Blanche speaks exclusively to two South African asylum seekers in Ireland, bringing the contorversial subject of immigration into sharp focus with a unique South African lense.

Summary:
In the last decade, thousands of South Africans have quietly sought asylum in Europe. Their claims span political persecution, targeted gang violence, and sexual orientation-based discrimination. Yet South Africa remains a constitutional democracy — and is officially listed as a safe country of origin by many European states, including Ireland.
So what’s driving the surge in asylum applications? Are genuine victims falling through the cracks of a rigid system — or are some South Africans exploiting legal grey areas in an increasingly overstretched asylum regime? Essentially: Are these South Africans claiming asylum or taking advantage?
Carte Blanche travels to Ireland, a country now central to this unfolding dilemma, to meet those navigating — and questioning — the boundaries of protection, policy and personal truth.
From here, we dig into the core question: Are South Africans genuinely at risk — or manipulating asylum frameworks for the opportunity to escape the world’s most unequal society? Moreover, this reports presents a chance to illustrate how differently systems treat the same nationality, depending on postcode and political pressure. And how South Africans can also be seen as the “other” in a growlingly toxic debate on who belongs where in the world of migration.

- 3 nights accommodation in Ireland
- 3 days shooting with local camera at 550 euros a day

Press Release:


Borderline Claims

Are South Africans fleeing danger, or gaming Europe’s asylum system? In the last decade, thousands of South Africans have sought asylum in Ireland. They claim they’re fleeing gang violence, crime and discrimination. But South Africa is officially listed as a safe country of origin by Ireland. As refugees face pushback from movements protesting provision of scarce housing and government resources to immigrants, some families face deportation. Are genuine victims falling through the cracks of a rigid system — or are some South Africans exploiting legal grey areas in an overstretched asylum system?

Producer & Presenter: Nickolaus Bauer

Script:


(ALFRED)
I wanted to give everybody just a better and brighter future,

(LUKE O’ CONNOR)
There is an incestuous web of corruption taking place in Ireland. When it comes to immigration.

(LUCKY KHAMBULE)
Once deportation is issued, you must know that at any time it can be implemented,

(SHANE RYAN)
It's horrible. Like, you were described as being racist! They just don't see what's happening in the villages.

(ANGELIQUE RADEMEYER)
So many asylum seekers. They have come in undocumented. Causing so much chaos. Why are they not sending those people back? Why are they sending the South Africans back?

(PHILLIP KINANE)
A generous nation, kind nation. And we've shown that. But I think it's been abused now.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Alfred doesn’t want to be identified. A South African asylum seekers staying in Wicklow, in the East of Ireland. In International Protection Accommodation paid for by the Irish government.

(ALFRED)
I come from a neighbourhood where gangsterism is rife. On a daily basis, you know, we hear people getting shot. We hear people being killed. A few times myself have been threatened with my life. South Africa has normalised this life that we that we live.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
In 2022 Alfred fled to Ireland. Fearing for his safety and wanting to build a better life for himself and his family. Initially trying to study he claimed asylum after his student visa was rejected. He now shares this two bedroomed apartment with 5 other asylum seekers from around the world while his application is being processed.

(ALFRED)
I feel like I'm in prison because I'm confined to this place. I can't work. I'm stuck in this place until, the government decides otherwise.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Alfred is just one of over one hundred thousand that have claimed asylum in the past five years in Ireland. A nation of just over five million. Fuelling a fierce debate around immigration in the country.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Lucky Khambule of the Movement for Asylum Seekers in Ireland is from Kwazulu-Natal and claimed asylum in 2012 after witnessing a political killing in Kwamashu. He was eventually declared a refugee after 4 years and is now an Irish citizen.

(LUCKY KHAMBULE - MOVEMENT FOR ASYLUM SEEKERS IN IRELAND)

It is an obligation of the Irish state to take care of any individual who feels unsafe where they come from, even if they are from South Africa.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Claiming asylum in Ireland is straightforward. You present yourself to what’s called the International Protection Office in Dublin and declare you feel unsafe in your home country for political, social or security reasons. The Irish government then considers your application. Asylum seekers usually aren’t allowed to work. But the government provides accommodation, vouchers for food and a weekly stipend of thirty eight EUROS - or roughly R780. Until it decides if they qualify to become a refugee and eventually an Irish citizen. Over 1000 South Africans have sought asylum in Ireland annually for the past two years.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
But now, a country once seen as welcoming to refugees is facing a political backlash. And government is feeling the pressure Kilkenny activist Luke O’ Connor believes Ireland is being taken advantage of.

(LUKE O’ CONNOR)
We're handing out citizenship like confetti. You know, we've actually debased our own citizenship by making it so easy to get.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
The Irish government does not have enough housing for asylum applicants.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
And these are dotted all over Kilkenny?

(LUKE O’ CONNOR)
All over the county and the wider country

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
To meet demand they’ve repurposed public property and entered into fastracked contracts with private sector to house asylum applicants in International Protection Accommodation Services like this - also known as IPAS Centres.

An IPAS centre is the accommodation given to asylum seekers by the Irish government while they process their application.

(LUKE O’ CONNOR)
This used to be a community centre, for the local area. It was refused commercial planning for a shop slash cafe. And, after it was refused art, it became an IPAS centre under the planning exemption.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
You were telling me that there's hotels that become IPAS centres? Can you show me one?

(LUKE O’ CONNOR)
We'll show you one. Yeah. Okay.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
How many hotels like this have been turned into Ipas centres.

(LUKE O’ CONNOR)
There's there's definitely 50 to 60 around the country. There's a lot of communities that might have only had one, kind of guest slash community centre. And that's become an IPAS centre.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
The rapid expansion of IPAS centers has led to an outcry from Irish citizens. Dundrum - a rural community of just over two hundred in Tipperary have protested for over 400 days. After 80 asylum seekers were put up at the local golf course in . With plans to increase numbers to 270 - far outnumbering the local population - they prevented more arriving by manning the entrance twenty four hours a day..

(VOX POP 1)
This community is being overrun. They are talking about bringing 270 in here with this say that after a period of time, those people are allowed to think five in 7 or 1 family in as well.

(VOX POP 2)

It's too much. It's too much. And it's pushing Irish people out.

(VOX POP 3)

When the natives become a minority in any community, any country. It's never good, never good for the natives. History has taught us that.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Dundrum and communities like it around Ireland are demanding more action and transparency from their government on immigration. And to prioritise services to indigenous Irish communities over asylum seekers. Especially social housing as homelessness has increased by 400% in the past decade.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER - PTC)
There's not enough housing in Ireland. The country needs an extra 250,000 homes. But the rate of voting simply can't meet that demand. Fuelling debate about who the government should be providing housing to.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
IPAS centers are also exempt from the strict planning laws that slow housing development in the country. So building a cottage in your backyard could take years for approval. While accommodation for asylum seekers can spring up in weeks. Adding to the rising anger against immigration.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
South Africa is designated as a safe country by the Irish justice system. Meaning South Africans can still lodge applications for asylum. But there is a higher chance they will be rejected and asked to leave.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
The Rademeyers and Pinards - originally from Springs in Gauteng - are being deported.

***INSERT UPSOUND***

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)

Fed up with crime and living in fear, the Rademeyers arrived in August 2022 and the Pinards arrived in May 2023.

The Angeliue and Caspar Rademeyer no longer receive benefits after being granted work permits. And have built themselves up in Longford. Where her Mom Yolinda and brother Arend Pinard - still in IPAS accommodation in Ballycastle - are visiting.

Despite having been victims of crime - the Irish government found their application for asylum lacked sufficient evidence to prove they are unsafe in their home country.

***ESTABLISHING SHOT IN LOUNGE***

(YOLINDA PINARD)
I won't go back to South Africa.
They actually assaulted me. I was nearly raped, and that was my last straw. There's, just too much going on at home. There's just too much crime, and, I won't be able to handle it.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
There's lots of South Africans that are victims of crime, but they're not claiming asylum?

(AREND PINARD)
That constant fear and living in that. It's not living. It's surviving.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
And the decision to come to Ireland?

(AREND PINARD)
Well, Ireland was taking asylum seekers I was seeking asylum out of my own country. And that's a country that I love. You know, I love braaing, I love 4x4ing, I love fishing, you know, I love the bush.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Surely if South Africa is such a great place, you stay back in South Africa and fight for it?

(AREND PINARD)
Yeah, And I would. But it's not just for me. For my kids. You know, I wouldn't want anything to happen to them.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
How do you feel about the Irish people considering you a burden on their society?They think you're here for a free ride?

(AREND PINARD)
Yeah, I would be angry as well. I never wanted to come here and just live off the government and live in their accommodation. It that wasn't my plan. I wanted to start working, contribute to the country, live in my own house. Live. I didn't want any of this.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Both families have appealed their deportations. And need to report to the local police station every three months for a stay of execution while that appeal is dealt with. But they could be sent home immediately.

(ANGELIQUE RADEMEYER)

The deportation is right here at the door. At the door. But there's nothing we can do and nothing you can do.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Are you determined as well that you won't go back to South Africa?

(ANGELIQUE RADEMEYER)
We'll never go back to South Africa. We have six beautiful children and, two of our children are with us in Ireland. My in-laws were deported back to South Africa. We doing this for our kids because even though they might not see it now, a time is going to come and that they gonna want to get out. I just feel that there's no future for us, especially for the white people in South Africa anymore.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Ireland deports on average only 1000 asylum seekers a year. But the new Irish coalition government that came to power in January this year has deployed 100 police officers specifically for immigration enforcement. Its a sign of growing public anger towards migration. Not only in Ireland but all over Europe.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER - PTC)
At the heart of Europe's immigration challenges is the Schengen border free system, which enables visa free travel between member states. It means that people can move freely between two countries without declaring themselves goods, or even showing their passports. Ireland may be separated from the European mainland by a sea, but it shares a border with northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom. I just passed that border, illustrating just how simple it is in this part of the world. The slip between two countries.

While approximately twenty thousand claim asylum in Ireland each year… A million do so in Europe annually. Politicians and the public are starting to blame Schengen’s lax border controls for those numbers. And public sentiment towards refugees and asylum seekers is turning bitter.

(LUKE O’ CONNOR)
If the issue isn't dealt with, you're going to see an increasingly combustible social and political situation where the genie can't go back into the bottle, you'll have civil disobedience.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Even though they seem to be living on borrowed time… These South Africans refuse to budge.

(ANGELIQUE RADEMEYER)
Its ridiculous because we are both working. Paying tax. We are getting nothing. We've integrated into this country. So I don't know what that is, but we're not giving up.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
What do you say to the people that are accusing you of being a chance taker, someone that's coming, and trying to enter Ireland through the back door?

(ALFRED)
I don't want the government to give me anything, demanding anything. I'm just asking for a chance just to be a human being. To be allowed to live a normal life, to be safe and and just to be human.

VOICEOVER:
They fled for their safety
Arend Pinard
“That constant fear and living in that. I couldn't take it anymore”
Only to be told to return.
LUCKY KHAMBULE:
“The government here has deemed South Africa a safe country.
Amid an immigration backlash
PHILLIP KINANE:
“There has to be a time to say enough is enough. You have to look after your own people.”



Promo 2

ANGELIQUE RADEMEYER:
Why are they sending the South Africans back?”
Locals say they’ve reached a breaking point
PHILLIP KINANE:
If you look at the numbers, the demographics we’ve been pushed out, that’s what’s happening.
But deportation is not an option.
ALFRED:
“This government can fight me all they want… I will fight till the very end.”

Promo 3
VOICEOVER:
They came to Ireland seeking safety
LUKE O’CONNOR:
“I don’t think we have a responsibility to take anyone who claims to be an asylum seeker.”
VOICEOVER:
They believe their fears are justified.
LUCKY KHAMBULE
“Those fears have been tested and found to be true.”
But they are being deported
YOLINDA PINARD:
“I don’t want to be treated like a criminal.”
VOICEOVER:
Why are they being sent back to South Africa?

Until it decides if they qualify to become a refugee and eventually an Irish citizen. Over 1000 South Africans have sought asylum in Ireland annually for the past two years. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) But now, a country once seen as welcoming to refugees is facing a political backlash. And government is feeling the pressure Kilkenny activist Luke O’ Connor believes Ireland is being taken advantage of. (LUKE O’ CONNOR) We're handing out citizenship like confetti. You know, we've actually debased our own citizenship by making it so easy to get. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) The Irish government does not have enough housing for asylum applicants. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) And these are dotted all over Kilkenny? (LUKE O’ CONNOR) All over the county and the wider country (NICKOLAUS BAUER) To meet demand they’ve repurposed public property and entered into fastracked contracts with private sector to house asylum applicants in International Protection Accommodation Services like this - also known as IPAS Centres. An IPAS centre is the accommodation given to asylum seekers by the Irish government while they process their application. (LUKE O’ CONNOR) This used to be a community centre, for the local area. It was refused commercial planning for a shop slash cafe. And, after it was refused art, it became an IPAS centre under the planning exemption. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) You were telling me that there's hotels that become IPAS centres? Can you show me one? (LUKE O’ CONNOR) We'll show you one. Yeah. Okay. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) How many hotels like this have been turned into Ipas centres. (LUKE O’ CONNOR) There's there's definitely 50 to 60 around the country. There's a lot of communities that might have only had one, kind of guest slash community centre. And that's become an IPAS centre. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) The rapid expansion of IPAS centers has led to an outcry from Irish citizens. Dundrum - a rural community of just over two hundred in Tipperary have protested for over 400 days. After 80 asylum seekers were put up at the local golf course in . With plans to increase numbers to 270 - far outnumbering the local population - they prevented more arriving by manning the entrance twenty four hours a day.. (VOX POP 1) This community is being overrun. They are talking about bringing 270 in here with this say that after a period of time, those people are allowed to think five in 7 or 1 family in as well. (VOX POP 2) It's too much. It's too much. And it's pushing Irish people out. (VOX POP 3) When the natives become a minority in any community, any country. It's never good, never good for the natives. History has taught us that. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Dundrum and communities like it around Ireland are demanding more action and transparency from their government on immigration. And to prioritise services to indigenous Irish communities over asylum seekers. Especially social housing as homelessness has increased by 400% in the past decade. (NICKOLAUS BAUER - PTC) There's not enough housing in Ireland. The country needs an extra 250,000 homes. But the rate of voting simply can't meet that demand. Fuelling debate about who the government should be providing housing to. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) IPAS centers are also exempt from the strict planning laws that slow housing development in the country. So building a cottage in your backyard could take years for approval. While accommodation for asylum seekers can spring up in weeks. Adding to the rising anger against immigration. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) South Africa is designated as a safe country by the Irish justice system. Meaning South Africans can still lodge applications for asylum. But there is a higher chance they will be rejected and asked to leave. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) The Rademeyers and Pinards - originally from Springs in Gauteng - are being deported. ***INSERT UPSOUND*** (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Fed up with crime and living in fear, the Rademeyers arrived in August 2022 and the Pinards arrived in May 2023. The Angeliue and Caspar Rademeyer no longer receive benefits after being granted work permits. And have built themselves up in Longford. Where her Mom Yolinda and brother Arend Pinard - still in IPAS accommodation in Ballycastle - are visiting. Despite having been victims of crime - the Irish government found their application for asylum lacked sufficient evidence to prove they are unsafe in their home country. ***ESTABLISHING SHOT IN LOUNGE*** (YOLINDA PINARD) I won't go back to South Africa. They actually assaulted me. I was nearly raped, and that was my last straw. There's, just too much going on at home. There's just too much crime, and, I won't be able to handle it. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) There's lots of South Africans that are victims of crime, but they're not claiming asylum? (AREND PINARD) That constant fear and living in that. It's not living. It's surviving. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) And the decision to come to Ireland? (AREND PINARD) Well, Ireland was taking asylum seekers I was seeking asylum out of my own country. And that's a country that I love. You know, I love braaing, I love 4x4ing, I love fishing, you know, I love the bush. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Surely if South Africa is such a great place, you stay back in South Africa and fight for it? (AREND PINARD) Yeah, And I would. But it's not just for me. For my kids. You know, I wouldn't want anything to happen to them. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) How do you feel about the Irish people considering you a burden on their society?They think you're here for a free ride? (AREND PINARD) Yeah, I would be angry as well. I never wanted to come here and just live off the government and live in their accommodation. It that wasn't my plan. I wanted to start working, contribute to the country, live in my own house. Live. I didn't want any of this. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Both families have appealed their deportations. And need to report to the local police station every three months for a stay of execution while that appeal is dealt with. But they could be sent home immediately. (ANGELIQUE RADEMEYER) The deportation is right here at the door. At the door. But there's nothing we can do and nothing you can do. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Are you determined as well that you won't go back to South Africa? (ANGELIQUE RADEMEYER) We'll never go back to South Africa. We have six beautiful children and, two of our children are with us in Ireland. My in-laws were deported back to South Africa. We doing this for our kids because even though they might not see it now, a time is going to come and that they gonna want to get out. I just feel that there's no future for us, especially for the white people in South Africa anymore. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Ireland deports on average only 1000 asylum seekers a year. But the new Irish coalition government that came to power in January this year has deployed 100 police officers specifically for immigration enforcement. Its a sign of growing public anger towards migration. Not only in Ireland but all over Europe. (NICKOLAUS BAUER - PTC) At the heart of Europe's immigration challenges is the Schengen border free system, which enables visa free travel between member states. It means that people can move freely between two countries without declaring themselves goods, or even showing their passports. Ireland may be separated from the European mainland by a sea, but it shares a border with northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom. I just passed that border, illustrating just how simple it is in this part of the world. The slip between two countries. While approximately twenty thousand claim asylum in Ireland each year… A million do so in Europe annually. Politicians and the public are starting to blame Schengen’s lax border controls for those numbers. And public sentiment towards refugees and asylum seekers is turning bitter. (LUKE O’ CONNOR) If the issue isn't dealt with, you're going to see an increasingly combustible social and political situation where the genie can't go back into the bottle, you'll have civil disobedience. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Even though they seem to be living on borrowed time… These South Africans refuse to budge. (ANGELIQUE RADEMEYER) Its ridiculous because we are both working. Paying tax. We are getting nothing. We've integrated into this country. So I don't know what that is, but we're not giving up. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) What do you say to the people that are accusing you of being a chance taker, someone that's coming, and trying to enter Ireland through the back door? (ALFRED) I don't want the government to give me anything, demanding anything. I'm just asking for a chance just to be a human being. To be allowed to live a normal life, to be safe and and just to be human. Promo 1 VOICEOVER: They fled for their safety Arend Pinard “That constant fear and living in that. I couldn't take it anymore” Only to be told to return. LUCKY KHAMBULE: “The government here has deemed South Africa a safe country. Amid an immigration backlash PHILLIP KINANE: “There has to be a time to say enough is enough. You have to look after your own people.” Promo 2 VOICEOVER: Seeking asylum, they’ve been told to leave ANGELIQUE RADEMEYER: Why are they sending the South Africans back?” Locals say they’ve reached a breaking point PHILLIP KINANE: If you look at the numbers, the demographics we’ve been pushed out, that’s what’s happening. But deportation is not an option. ALFRED: “This government can fight me all they want… I will fight till the very end.” Promo 3 VOICEOVER: They came to Ireland seeking safety LUKE O’CONNOR: “I don’t think we have a responsibility to take anyone who claims to be an asylum seeker.” VOICEOVER: They believe their fears are justified. LUCKY KHAMBULE “Those fears have been tested and found to be true.” But they are being deported YOLINDA PINARD: “I don’t want to be treated like a criminal.” VOICEOVER: Why are they being sent back to South Africa?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Are South Africans fleeing danger — or gaming Europe’s asylum system to escape inequality at home?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Carte Blanche speaks exclusively to two South African asylum seekers in Ireland, bringing the contorversial subject of immigration into sharp focus with a unique South African lense.
metadata.Summary: In the last decade, thousands of South Africans have quietly sought asylum in Europe. Their claims span political persecution, targeted gang violence, and sexual orientation-based discrimination. Yet South Africa remains a constitutional democracy — and is officially listed as a safe country of origin by many European states, including Ireland. So what’s driving the surge in asylum applications? Are genuine victims falling through the cracks of a rigid system — or are some South Africans exploiting legal grey areas in an increasingly overstretched asylum regime? Essentially: Are these South Africans claiming asylum or taking advantage? Carte Blanche travels to Ireland, a country now central to this unfolding dilemma, to meet those navigating — and questioning — the boundaries of protection, policy and personal truth. From here, we dig into the core question: Are South Africans genuinely at risk — or manipulating asylum frameworks for the opportunity to escape the world’s most unequal society? Moreover, this reports presents a chance to illustrate how differently systems treat the same nationality, depending on postcode and political pressure. And how South Africans can also be seen as the “other” in a growlingly toxic debate on who belongs where in the world of migration.
